title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Machine — Analog, Embedded Processing & Real-World Silicon

epigraph.quote: Every electronic system in the physical world needs two things before a single line of software can run: clean power and a bridge between real-world signals and digital logic.
epigraph.author: Analog Engineering Maxim

web_blocks.html: Headline AI chipmakers sell a handful of $30,000 processors to four cloud giants. Texas Instruments runs the opposite model. It sells roughly 80,000 distinct chip products to more than 100,000 buyers worldwide [1, 4]. TI reports two core operating segments—Analog and Embedded Processing—plus a small Other unit [1]. Every modern machine needs these chips. A factory robot, an electric car battery, and a cloud server rack all rely on TI parts. These parts regulate voltage, sense heat and current, isolate high-voltage rails, and run real-time control loops.

web_blocks.caption: Segment Revenue, Operating Profit & Margin Breakdown (FY2021–Q3 2026, $ Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: Analog generates ~79%–81% of revenue and ~87%–90% of segment operating profit, rebounding from a 37.9% trough margin in FY2024 to 51.0% in Q3 2026; Embedded Processing is recovering from an 11.3% margin trough in FY2025 to 26.5% in Q3 2026.

web_blocks.html: 1. Analog ($14,006M in FY2025, 79.2% of revenue; $4,911M in Q3 2026, 81.1% of revenue): Analog is TI's core profit engine [1, 2]. It covers two main product groups: Power and Signal Chain [1, 7]. Power chips include DC/DC switching regulators, AC/DC controllers, battery monitors, motor drivers, and gallium nitride (GaN) stages [1, 7]. Signal Chain chips include op-amps, data converters, interface transceivers, and isolation parts [1, 7]. Digital chips work only with ones and zeros. Analog chips handle real-world inputs like voltage, current, heat, pressure, and sound. Analog operating margin fell to 37.9% in FY2024 and 38.6% in FY2025 on low fab load and higher 300mm depreciation [1, 7]. As volume returned, margin snapped back to 51.0% in Q3 2026 [2].

Concrete End-to-End Analog Example — 800V Electric Vehicle Traction & Battery Management: Picture an automaker building an 800-volt electric SUV. Inside the battery pack, TI's BQ79616 monitor chip tracks cell voltage and heat across 16 or more cells in series. It reads values within a fraction of a millivolt and sends data over an isolated link to prevent thermal runaway. Downstream, in the charger and DC/DC converter, TI's UCC5880 gate drivers and 650V GaN power stages step 800V pack power down to 48V and 12V rails. Those rails run power steering, brakes, and cabin screens. One EV can hold $300 to $500+ of TI analog chips across dozens of qualified sockets. Those parts often stay in production for the vehicle's full 7-to-10-year platform life.

2. Embedded Processing ($2,697M in FY2025, 15.3% of revenue; $858M in Q3 2026, 14.2% of revenue): Embedded Processing sells microcontrollers (MCUs), digital signal processors (DSPs), and system processors [1, 7]. These chips run precise, real-time tasks inside physical machines [1, 7]. Embedded margins fell hard during the 2024–2025 slump, dropping from 38.4% in 2022 to 11.3% in FY2025 [1, 7]. That drop came from moving foundry wafers into TI's Lehi 300mm fab (LFAB1) while fab load stayed low [1, 4]. By Q3 2026, Embedded margin recovered to 26.5%, with $227M in operating profit on $858M in sales [2]. In February 2026, TI also agreed to buy Silicon Labs for $7.5 billion [6]. Expected to close in H1 2027, that deal adds ~1,200 wireless IoT chips covering Bluetooth LE, Zigbee, Thread, Matter, and Wi-Fi [6].

Concrete End-to-End Embedded Processing Example — Industrial Robotic Servo Drive & Edge Vision: Picture a smart factory running a 6-axis robot arm. At each joint, a TI C2000™ real-time MCU (such as the TMS320F28388D) checks motor current and position in nanoseconds. It runs fast control loops so the arm moves with micron-level accuracy. At the main hub, a TI Sitara™ AM64x or Jacinto™ TDA4x chip blends camera and LiDAR feeds to spot obstacles. That lets robots work safely near human staff. Customers write millions of lines of custom control code on TI's Code Composer Studio and C2000 tools. Switching to a rival MCU would force years of new coding and safety tests.

3. Other ($979M in FY2025, 5.5% of revenue; $286M in Q3 2026, 4.7% of revenue): The Other unit holds DLP® light chips, school calculators, custom ASICs, and corporate items such as restructuring costs [1, 2, 7]. Even at under 6% of sales, Other earned $307 million in operating profit in FY2025 (31.4% margin) [1]. In Q3 2026, it posted $142 million in operating profit, or a 49.7% margin [2]. This small unit acts as a steady cash earner while absorbing corporate items [1, 2].

Concrete End-to-End Other Segment Example — Automotive Head-Up Displays (DLP®) & STEM Calculators: Inside a luxury car's head-up display, a TI DLP5530-Q1 chip uses hundreds of thousands of tiny tilting aluminum mirrors. Those mirrors project clear turn arrows onto the windshield even in bright sun. Elsewhere, in North American high schools and colleges, TI's TI-84 Plus CE and TI-Nspire™ CX II calculators remain required tools for AP Calculus, SAT, and ACT exams. That classroom standard brings high-margin, repeat fall sales with very low R&D spend.

web_blocks.takeaway: Industrial and Automotive together account for 66% of TI's revenue, while the newly broken-out Data Center segment reached 9% in FY2025 as AI server power density increased analog content per rack.

web_blocks.html: Why Multi-Chip Board Content Compounds Switching Costs — and Where Concentration Exists: When an engineer builds a factory drive, medical scanner, or 48V AI server board, they rarely buy just one TI chip. A single printed circuit board often uses twenty to forty TI power and signal-chain parts. Those parts work together in pre-tested reference designs that meet strict thermal and noise rules. Even in Personal Electronics at 21% of revenue, TI sells across hundreds of device models [1]. Yet TI is not wholly immune to buyer concentration. Per Note 1 of the FY2025 Form 10-K, one unnamed end customer accounted for 12% of total revenue in both 2025 (~$2.12B) and 2024 (~$1.88B), mainly in Analog, up from under 10% in 2023 [1]. That single buyer represents roughly half of Personal Electronics sales, creating real order-swing risk if that OEM shifts power architectures in-house [1].

Data Center Power Growth & Long-Life Catalog Math: Data Center became a standalone 9% end market in FY2025 as AI server racks pushed past 100 kilowatts [1]. Higher rack power forces servers onto 48-volt power rails, multiplying demand for multiphase controllers, hot-swap eFuses, and smart power stages. Meanwhile, TI releases hundreds of new parts each year while retiring very few legacy SKUs [4]. Because industrial and auto designs stay in production for 10 to 20 years, each design win adds a durable layer of repeat orders [4, 7]. That steady layering turns TI's 80,000-part catalog into a broad cash-flow base.

Why Embedded Processing & Silicon Labs Fit Together: TI's Embedded Processing unit serves many of the same industrial and auto buyers as Analog [1, 4]. A factory controller or smart grid meter needs both a real-time microcontroller and an isolated power stage. By adding Silicon Labs' ~1,200 wireless IoT parts in H1 2027, TI can pair its C2000 and MSPM0 MCUs with Bluetooth LE, Zigbee, Thread, Matter, and Wi-Fi radios [6]. That combined stack lets customers source compute, wireless links, and power management from one direct TI.com account [4, 6].

Geographic Ship-To Concentration & Residual Distributor Risk: Geographic filings reveal a second concentration layer beyond end-market labels. By customer headquarters, the U.S. led at 39% ($2,348M) of Q3 2026 revenue, followed by China at 23% ($1,392M, up 36.6% YoY), EMEA at 20% ($1,207M, Germany 9%), Rest of Asia at 10% ($635M), and Japan at 6% ($369M) [2]. Because Western OEMs also assemble hardware in mainland factories, TI's FY2025 Form 10-K discloses that roughly 50% of 2025 revenue came from products physically shipped into China [1]. Meanwhile, less than 20% of revenue still flows through one global distributor and a few regional distributors, exposing that tail to competing line promotion and partner credit risk [1].

web_blocks.title: THE MIX INSIGHT
paragraphs: Fifteen years ago, Personal Electronics and Telecom drove most of TI's sales. Today, Industrial (33%), Automotive (33%), and Data Center (9%) make up 75% of revenue [1]. That mix shift steadies demand over a decade, though investors must watch two concentration points: one unnamed Analog buyer at 12% of FY2025 revenue, and China-headquartered accounts at 23% of Q3 2026 sales (~50% of 2025 shipments entering China factories) [1, 2].

book_paragraphs: When you pick up a phone or sit in an electric car, your eyes go straight to the screen or the main AI chip. Nobody thinks about the fifty tiny black chips around the edge of the board. Yet those parts keep the battery from catching fire, step 800 volts down to 1.2 volts, and turn heat and current into clean signals. That hidden layer of silicon is Texas Instruments' entire world.

Let's break down the three units TI reports so you know where every dollar of sales and profit comes from. The giant is Analog, which brought in $14.01 billion in 2025—nearly 80% of total sales—and $5.41 billion in operating profit. By Q3 2026, Analog ran at $4.91 billion a quarter with a 51.0% operating margin. Think of Analog as two toolkits: Power manages and converts electricity, while Signal Chain senses and cleans up physical signals.

To see Analog in action, picture an engineer designing an 800-volt electric SUV. Inside the battery pack, TI's BQ79616 monitor chip tracks the voltage and heat of each cell to stop thermal runaway. Out in the drivetrain and charger, TI's isolated gate drivers and GaN power stages step 800 volts down to 48-volt and 12-volt rails. Those rails run steering, brakes, and cabin screens. Once qualified for safety, that chip stays in the car platform for seven to ten years.

The second unit is Embedded Processing, which earned $2.70 billion in 2025 and $858 million in Q3 2026. These are the microcontrollers and signal processors that run real-time control loops. Inside a six-axis factory robot arm, a TI C2000 chip checks motor current in nanoseconds so the arm stops on a dime. Embedded margin fell to 11.3% in 2025 as TI moved wafers into its Lehi fab during a slump, then rebounded to 26.5% in Q3 2026. With the $7.5 billion Silicon Labs deal announced in February 2026, TI is adding 1,200 wireless IoT chips for Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and Thread.

The third unit is Other, with $979 million in 2025 sales and $286 million in Q3 2026. It sounds small, yet it houses TI's DLP mirror chips that project navigation arrows onto luxury car windshields. It also sells the TI-84 and TI-Nspire calculators that students buy every August. Even this small unit threw off $307 million in operating profit in 2025.

Beneath that 80,000-part catalog, investors still need to watch two hidden concentration points disclosed in TI's Form 10-K. First, one unnamed end customer accounted for 12% of total revenue in both 2024 and 2025, primarily in Analog. Second, while China-headquartered customers represent 23% of Q3 2026 revenue, about 50% of TI's 2025 products physically shipped into China for assembly.

book_subsections.title: Why End-Market Mix Matters
paragraphs: Look at who buys all these chips. In 2025, TI broke out Data Center as its own 9% end market, driven by AI server power demand. As rack power jumped from 15 kilowatts to over 100 kilowatts, data centers shifted to 48-volt power rails. That shift multiplied the count of multiphase controllers, hot-swap switches, and gate drivers inside each server. Alongside Data Center, Industrial makes up 33% of sales and Automotive adds another 33%. Personal Electronics sits at 21%, Communications at 3%, and Other at 1%.

Put Industrial, Automotive, and Data Center together and you get 75% of TI's total revenue. Those buyers care far more about reliability, ten-year supply, and power efficiency than saving two cents on a part. When an automaker qualifies a TI battery chip or a factory firm codes around a C2000 MCU, that socket stays locked in for a decade or more. The result is an annuity-like stream of high-margin repeat orders.

Just as important is separating SKU breadth from true customer dispersion. No single part number drives TI's revenue, yet Note 1 of the FY2025 Form 10-K reveals that one unnamed Analog end customer accounted for 12% of total sales in both 2024 and 2025 (roughly $2.12 billion in 2025), up from under 10% in 2023. Outside that 12% anchor buyer, the remaining 88% of revenue is spread across more than 100,000 accounts. Even in Data Center at 9% of FY2025 sales, TI sells the power plumbing needed inside every dense server rack rather than betting on one GPU winner.

The Embedded Processing rebound in 2026 also deserves close attention. After margins sank to 11.3% in FY2025 during the Lehi fab shift, Q3 2026 Embedded profit jumped to $227 million on $858 million of sales—a 26.5% margin. Adding Silicon Labs' ~1,200 low-power wireless chips in H1 2027 will let TI pair real-time C2000 and MSPM0 control with Bluetooth LE, Thread, Matter, and Wi-Fi on one board. That bundle makes TI's industrial and smart-building lineup much harder for niche rivals to displace.

Think about the customer math behind that catalog breadth. When a medical-device maker or factory supplier designs a new board, they rarely buy just one chip. They buy thirty or forty matching TI parts—voltage regulators, current amps, CAN transceivers, precision converters, and real-time MCUs—from TI's reference designs. Every extra TI socket on a board cuts the buyer's engineering time and raises the cost of switching to a rival.

Look also at how long industrial and auto sockets last. In phones, a power chip might ship for eighteen months before the next model replaces it. In a factory controller, medical scanner, or car powertrain, a qualified TI part often ships for ten to twenty years. Because TI runs its own 300mm fabs instead of relying on outside foundries that may close old nodes, industrial buyers treat TI as a long-term plant partner.

That long life creates a quiet compounding loop inside the catalog. Each year, TI launches hundreds of new analog and embedded parts tuned for higher voltage, tighter heat limits, or lower standby draw. At the same time, it retires very few older parts. Over decades, that catalog has grown to roughly 80,000 active SKUs serving over 100,000 customers. A rival cannot match TI simply by spending more on R&D for two years. They would have to rebuild eighty thousand qualified datasheets, software tools, and decades of buyer trust.

Even inside Personal Electronics—still 21% of sales—TI avoids single-socket traps by focusing on battery charging, display power, USB-C delivery, and audio amps across hundreds of models. Together, the two core segments and six end markets form one of the widest revenue bases in global tech.

Notice how that end-market diversity protects TI during uneven cycles. When smartphone demand cooled in 2023, automotive electrification and early AI power builds helped cushion the drop. In 2026, as industrial factory spending recovered alongside Data Center 48-volt upgrades, Analog operating profit jumped from $1.64 billion in Q1 to $2.51 billion in Q3. Few semiconductor companies can pull growth from factory floors, electric drivetrains, and hyperscale server racks all at the same time.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Analog is 80% of the business and nearly 90% of the profit, yet Embedded Processing and Data Center hold the biggest 2026 shifts. Watch whether Embedded margins climb back toward 30%+ once Lehi fills up and Silicon Labs closes.
